The vision of CityU’s Master of Counselling Program is to educate skilled, diverse, socially just

world experience into the classroom and emphasizes the core principles of reconciliation,

Course Description 
This course introduces students to research in the social sciences and provides them with the 
skills to critically review human wellness literature. Both qualitative and quantitative 
methodologies will be explored (e.g., autoethnography, indigenous methodologies, experimental 
design etc.). Proposals from this course may be further developed for later use in thesis and 
capstone research projects.

 What are the implications of the historical exploitation of vulnerable populations in 
scientific research?
 How can researchers ensure their work is respectful of non-dominant cultural norms?
 What does ethical, anti-oppressive research look like in practice?

Research Article Analysis-Group Presentation (assignment 1)            
In small groups (assigned randomly by the system), students will collaborate on 45–60-minute 
presentation analyzing an instructor-approved article. Presentation topics and preferred 
presentation dates must be submitted to the instructor by email for approval on a 
first-come, first-served basis. 
Beginning in Week 4 and continuing through Week 8, each group will present live in each 
class according to the order in which requests are received. The deadline to submit your 
article and preferred presentation day is before the second session Wednesday, July 8, 11:59 
pm. If no email is received from a group by the deadline, the instructor will assign that group 
to any remaining unselected date, which may include July 23, the first day of presentations. 
The email must include all group members’ emails, names, the group number (and presenting 
order), the PDF of selected article, and the preferred presentation date.
Each group will review and critically analyze a peer-reviewed research article that may report on 
either a quantitative or qualitative study. Using methodology-specific criteria, students will 
examine and discuss the following aspects of the study:
1) the research question and hypothesis; 2) the study design; 3) data analysis; 4) conclusions; 
5) clinical applications; and 6) ethics issues.
Students will consider the following questions in their analysis: 1) Is the design appropriate for 
the research question or hypothesis? 2) Are the population and sampling techniques 
appropriate? 3) Were issues of reliability and validity addressed, including the adequacy of the 
controls used? 4) are the researcher’s conclusions robustly supported by the data? 5) what 
alternative interpretations can be drawn from the data?
Students are encouraged to explore a range of presentation modalities including Powerpoint 
slides, spoken word poetry, dramatic skits, animation, monologues, videos, storytelling, music, 
dance, improv, collage, scrapbooking, story boarding, sculpture, quilting, papier-mâché, 
mandalas, painting, drawing, puppetry etc.
Group members will have to meet with their groups online to plan their presentation including 
scenario, characters, script, etc.
After presenting, each group is required to upload its slides in PPT format to ensure visibility of 
presenter notes (a brief summary of what you intend to say for each specific slide) to the 
discussion forum for other groups to review by midnight on the day of their presentations, 
and also submit the same file in the assignment submission area for the instructor to grade.

In consultation with their instructor, students will design a research study using a topic that could 
potentially serve as a capstone project. The paper will include: 1) a research question; 2) the

areas of literature; 5) eight to ten scholarly sources; 6) research variables; 7) the study 
methodology; 8) the data collection procedure; and 9) the method of analysis. 
This paper will include an ethics proposal that could be submitted to the university’s Institutional

                                                  Sensitive Content Notice            
Because the counselling profession is designed to explore the inner life of individuals, certain 
content discussed in CityU’s Master of Counselling courses may be emotionally activating for 
students. The university’s goal is to empower students to practice active self-care throughout 
their time in the program. Active self-care is an ethical responsibility for those in self-regulating 
professions and assists clinicians in successfully meeting clients in spaces where emotionally 
sensitive content is present. Similarly, in the Master of Counselling program, an ethic of care for 
the self is a critical consideration.
Emotionally sensitive content involves a wide variety of topics including, but not limited to, 
abuse, assault, neglect, self-harm, identity, sexuality, appearance, misogyny, classism, 
racialized issues, colonization, religious practices, trauma, grieving, ageism, caregiving, and 
physical or mental health. Students are encouraged to carefully attend to their emotional 
wellbeing when reading, listening to, viewing, or participating in course activities involving 
sensitive content. 
It is important to note that exploring sensitive content is an inherent part of the counselling 
profession. However, the complexity of human experience means students’ personal histories 
may become activated to the point that effective learning is no longer feasible. In such cases, 
students are encouraged to prioritize balancing their emotional wellbeing with their professional 
growth. This may be done through timely self-reflection and communication with instructors 
and/or peers about the self-regulation strategies students will implement while engaging 
sensitive content. 
As part of their professional growth, students are also encouraged to pursue personal 
counselling related to sensitive content explored in the program. Personal counselling deepens 
students’ learning and provides insight into their future clients’ experiences of the therapeutic 
process. Additional resources available to students include the Empower Me Program, Self-
Care folders in Brightspace, and local campus wellness initiatives
